content: Women who test positive for HPV during primary screening and are triage-positive are referred for colposcopy. Those who are triage-positive based on visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) are treated accordingly. Women who test positive for HPV types 16/18 are treated only if they are also triage-positive using VIA. Similarly, women with other high-risk HPV (OHR) types are treated only if they are triage-positive. When considering health-adjusted life years (HALYs) and cost-effectiveness, primary HPV screening without triage at 10-year intervals for women aged 35–45 years (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio [ICER] = $154 per HALY saved), 10-year intervals for ages 30–50 years (ICER = $393 per HALY saved), or 5-year intervals for ages 30–50 years (ICER = $502 per HALY saved) were identified as cost-effective strategies. Primary HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping triage at equivalent intervals was found to have similar cost-effectiveness outcomes compared to primary HPV screening without triage. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), where the average GDP per capita is $1,999, primary HPV screening every 5 years for women aged 30–50 years is considered cost-effective. Among the 78 LMICs analyzed, 68 countries (87%) have a GDP above $502, making 5-yearly HPV screening a viable option. For countries with lower willingness-to-pay thresholds, 10-yearly screening intervals may be more appropriate. When a 3% discount rate is applied to both costs and effects, primary HPV screening without triage at 10-year intervals for ages 35–45 years (ICER = $468 per HALY saved), 10-year intervals for ages 30–50 years (ICER = $1,089 per HALY saved), or 5-year intervals for ages 30–50 years (ICER = $1,453 per HALY saved) remains cost-effective. HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping triage at similar intervals also demonstrates comparable cost-effectiveness. For a willingness-to-pay threshold of $500 per HALY saved, only 10-yearly primary HPV screening at ages 35 and 45 years is cost-effective for 68 of the 78 LMICs. For countries with a GDP above $1,000 per capita, 10-yearly screening at ages 35–45 years or 30–50 years is cost-effective for 59 of the 78 LMICs (76%). Under scenarios with lower screening compliance, 5-yearly HPV screening becomes more cost-effective, as 68 LMICs have a GDP above $376, making this strategy feasible for most settings. HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping triage results in 36% fewer precancer treatment events, a 31% lower number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent a cervical cancer death, and 29% fewer adverse obstetric outcomes compared to primary HPV screening without triage. The average discounted cost per woman over a lifetime ranges from $3 for no screening to $21–$42 for 10-yearly screening, $39–$61 for 5-yearly screening, and up to $51–$80 for 3-yearly screening. The most cost-effective strategies, with a willingness-to-pay threshold of ~$500 per HALY saved, include 5-yearly screening for ages 30–50 years using primary HPV screening without triage or with 16/18 genotyping triage. These strategies have similar effectiveness and costs over a lifetime. Women managed under primary HPV screening with 16/18 genotyping triage experience 31% fewer precancer treatment events and 23% fewer adverse obstetric outcomes compared to those managed under primary HPV screening without triage. The NNT to prevent one cervical cancer death is 57 for primary HPV screening without triage and 40 for 16/18 genotyping triage, representing a 29% improvement. For women with a positive HPV test but a negative triage result, follow-up management strategies include retesting with HPV at 12 months (baseline), 24 months, or both 12 and 24 months. Retesting at 24 months alone may reduce precancer treatments with minimal loss of effectiveness, particularly for 16/18 genotyping or colposcopy triage. However, for VIA or cytology triage, retesting at 24 months instead of 12 months may result in a slight loss of effectiveness. The World Health Organization (WHO) suggests that women in the general population who test positive for HPV during primary screening and are triage-negative with 16/18 genotyping or colposcopy should be retested with HPV at 24 months, if feasible. If the follow-up HPV test is negative, these women can return to the regular screening interval.
